summary: The town pauses land-use approval processing for data storage facilities, including building permits and occupancy certificates. Applications submitted before July 1, 2026 may proceed. The pause runs 180 days from adoption and filing; an additional 180 days requires a Board resolution.
locator: Zoning Code, art. XX §§20.3, 20.9–20.10; L.L. 5-2026 (added August 25)
evidence: Any applications submitted to the Town of Orangetown

summary: Data centers require a conditional use permit in B-D and L-I; they are a permitted use in G-I. The R-1 and R-M cells are blank. This land-use classification does not itself issue a construction permit.
locator: Ordinance 26-652, §3, Exhibit B (PDF p. 14); QMC §20.40.010, district use chart

summary: In the area governed by the county’s East Wenatchee urban growth area zoning, site design, construction and operation of data centers, including cooling equipment, must meet the cited environmental noise limits at or beyond the boundary or where adjacent buildings are affected.
locator: DCC Title 18A, East Wenatchee UGA zoning, §18A.72.270(G)
evidence: beyond the property line or affecting adjacent buildings

summary: The East Wenatchee urban growth area design standards for blank walls apply to new data center structures under this county title except those in the general industrial zoning district.
locator: DCC Title 18A, East Wenatchee UGA zoning, §18A.72.270(F)

summary: Franklin Township in Gloucester County prohibits data centers in all zoning districts. The definition includes remote computing and cloud facilities; an in-person computer lab or workstation facility is separately defined. This is not the identically named Somerset County township.
locator: Ordinance O-5-2026, §§1–2, code §§253-3 and 253-96(G), p. 2; adoption cross-check NJ Pinelands Commission
evidence: listed prohibited use as subsection G

summary: Walton County’s land development code bars large-load customers, expressly including data centers as defined by Florida Chapter 2026-65, across its land-use categories and zoning districts. The general provision rules out variances. This describes county code; it does not establish a municipal rule.
authority: Walton County Board of County Commissioners
evidence: no variances hereto shall be permitted

summary: For facilities classified as computer infrastructure, data processing or web hosting, applications for a zoning action, special use, variance, land disturbance or building permit must include project and utility phasing timelines and a master site plan identifying parcel changes.
locator: County UDC, Aug. 2026 edition, §352(b)(1)–(3), printed p. 352-1 (PDF p. 277)

summary: Facilities cannot share a parcel boundary with residentially used or residentially zoned land. Within 200 feet of such land, maintain a 100-foot undisturbed buffer unless the director accepts a demonstrated site-design basis for reducing it. This is county land-use jurisdiction.
locator: County UDC §352(c)(1)–(2)(a), printed p. 352-1 (PDF p. 277)

summary: Charlotte and its extraterritorial jurisdiction pause applications for new telecommunications and data storage facilities beginning November 6, 2026. The extension ends upon new rules or October 18, 2027, whichever comes first. State-law exemptions also remain.
locator: Oct. 26 extension, §§1, 2(2)–(3), 6, pp. 2–4; Council matter 30195

summary: The moratorium exempts facilities primarily supporting internal operations of an institution, government, healthcare or telecom provider, or another permitted principal use, if they do not primarily provide processing to off-site users. This exception does not waive underlying zoning or construction requirements.
locator: Oct. 26 extension, §1, p. 2; Council matter 30195
evidence: not offered as a primary service

summary: The interim study pauses new/expanded data-center applications, rezonings and use permits for primary digital-data facilities using more than 20 MW or proposed within 500 feet of residentially zoned or residentially guided property. It ends February 17, 2027 unless the council ends it earlier.
locator: Interim-use ordinance, City Code §12.09(B), (D), (F)(2)–(5), pp. 1–3; Feb. 17 minutes

summary: The building-permit pause preserves specified repair, tenant improvement and commercial-building exceptions. An existing or approved data center may install equipment or build/expand under the listed exception only if the improvement will not allow use above 9 MW.
locator: Interim-use ordinance, City Code §12.09(F)(1)(i)–(iv), p. 2
Ordinance 2026-22 §II; County Code §72-301, packet pp. 26–27; final adoption Oct. 20
evidence: anticipated monthly peak load of 50 megawatts or more
summary: Unincorporated Volusia bars a single site with an anticipated monthly peak electric load of at least 50 MW, measured as the highest 15-minute average. The county may not accept, process or grant approvals for its development, expansion, intensification or operation. Incorporated municipalities are outside this rule.

locator: Code §138-5.301(b), Ordinance Extension, pp. 1–2; adopted by RES0224-2026, August 24 minutes p. 6
evidence: site plan approval on or before February 23, 2026
summary: The city added 180 days to the data-center development moratorium previously scheduled to end September 5, 2026. It exempts a development or building with approved site plans or complete plans submitted for site-plan approval by February 23, 2026. Earlier repeal remains possible.

locator: Signed Ordinance 127447 §§2–4, pp. 3–5
summary: All city zones pause applications to establish or expand a covered data center or change to that use, including accessory uses. The definition requires capacity over 20 MVA, a primary data-handling purpose and characteristic supporting infrastructure. The pause lasts 365 days from effectiveness unless shortened or extended.

locator: Signed Ordinance 127447 §2, p. 4
evidence: by no more than an additional 20
summary: A facility already operating when the ordinance took effect may apply for an expansion of up to 20 additional MVA if it meets the data-center definition or fails that definition only because its existing capacity is 20 MVA or less. This is an exemption from the pause, not an approval.

locator: Executive Order 62 (July 14, 2026), Data Center Permitting Moratorium and Generic Environmental Impact Statement; Definitions
evidence: does not apply to permits, approvals, licenses
summary: New York directs DEC to hold incomplete discretionary applications for construction or expansion of covered data centers capable of using at least 50 MW until DPS submits its final environmental impact report and findings. Existing complete applications and local government approvals are outside the order. Its definition excludes primarily manufacturing, research, educational and medical-care facilities.

locator: May 13, 2026 Town Board minutes, 08:47 moratorium motion; §4, pp. 17–18
summary: The town pauses applications for zoning, special-use, building, subdivision and site-plan approvals for data centers and commercial crypto mining. It covers all town real property for one year from effectiveness unless repealed sooner. A hardship variance may be sought under §7.

locator: May 13, 2026 Town Board minutes, 08:47 moratorium motion; §6, p. 18
summary: A duly approved facility already operating lawfully, with required permits, may continue as a nonconforming use. The protection does not cover expansion. This is the Town of Oneonta, not the separately incorporated city.

locator: Signed Ordinance 26-6-3 §IV; Appendix A §VII, Data Centers (a), (a)(i), PDF p. 2
summary: Facilities using on-site primary generation for continuous normal operations are limited to M-2, with the district’s special provisions also applying to generation equipment and fuel storage. In M-1, independent emergency or redundant power during loss of primary power is allowed subject to the supplemental rules.

locator: Signed Ordinance 26-6-3 §IV; Appendix A §VII, Data Centers (b), (c)(i), PDF p. 2
summary: Primary buildings and equipment must stand at least 300 feet from residential zoning and from school/daycare, assisted-living/nursing and park property boundaries. Lower-intensity accessory uses such as offices or parking may occupy that area. Adjacent sites require a planted buffer at least 25 feet deep, which may count toward the setback.

locator: Signed Ordinance 26-6-3 §IV; Appendix A §VII, Data Centers (c)(v)–(vii), PDF p. 3
summary: The permit requires a landscape plan stamped by a licensed landscape architect or landscape horticulturist. After installing the buffer, submit a signed completion certificate from the designer of record. The buffer must be maintained and does not replace standard parish landscaping.

locator: Signed Ordinance 26-6-3 §IV; Appendix A §VII, Data Centers (e)(i)–(ii), PDF p. 3
summary: Noise must not exceed 55 dBA at a property line adjacent to a residential or noise-sensitive area. In the adjacency settings specified in §VII(e), backup generator and similar equipment testing is restricted to weekdays, 7 a.m.–6 p.m.

locator: Signed Ordinance 26-6-3 §IV; Appendix A §VII, Data Centers (d)(i)–(iv), PDF p. 3
summary: Screen cooling, ventilation, backup generation and other operating equipment from public roadways and specified residential, school/daycare, care and park uses. The ordinance lists enclosures, buildings, opaque fencing or walls, and landscape buffers as possible methods.

locator: Zoning Regulations, Appendix A, permitted uses table; NAICS 518, legend and district column heads
evidence: Data Processing, Internet Providers & Web Search Portals
summary: The broad NAICS 518 data-processing category is marked permitted in C-1, C-2, O-I and M-1; M-2 and the residential columns are blank. The city specifically identifies M-1 as permitting its data-center projects. The industry row is not an automatic determination that every project component or another NAICS category qualifies.

locator: Signed Ordinance 151, Series 2026, §§I, III, p. 2; signatures p. 3
summary: Louisville Metro staff and named planning and adjustment boards pause rezoning, conditional use and Plan Certain Category 2B and 3 development plans proposing data centers or telecommunications hotels. Applications already scheduled for a public hearing at effectiveness may continue. The 180-day period can end on final permanent rules, repeal or extension.

locator: Signed Ordinance 151, Series 2026, §§II–III, p. 2; signatures p. 3
summary: Metro staff also pause acceptance and further processing of building-permit applications to repurpose existing structures for a data center or telecommunications hotel. This provision targets adaptive reuse; it is not a blanket ban on all construction by every city in Jefferson County.
